claims.text: Conventionally cast equiatomic FeCoNi-based alloy solidifies in the FCC phase.
The as-cast FeCoNi-based baseline has high saturation magnetization.
The as-cast FeCoNi-based baseline has low coercivity and exhibits soft ferromagnetism.
Severe plastic deformation will reduce the alloy's grain size to the nanometer scale.
Annealing at approximately 650°C for one hour will relieve processing stresses without significant grain growth.
SPD followed by controlled low-temperature annealing will create a stable nanocrystalline FeCoNi-based microstructure.
Nanocrystalline refinement will increase the density of grain boundaries and associated defects.
Fine grain boundaries and associated defects act as domain-wall pinning sites.
The increased density of grain boundaries hinders domain-wall motion during magnetization reversal.
Enhanced domain-wall pinning raises the coercive field.
SPD and annealing will increase coercivity relative to the coarse-grained, as-cast FeCoNi-based FCC baseline.
The processed alloy will retain high saturation magnetization.
The increased coercivity depends on avoiding excessive grain growth and unwanted phase transformations during annealing.
Significant coarsening or secondary-phase formation may prevent the coercivity increase.
The magnitude of the coercivity increase depends on the SPD and annealing parameters and on competing stress-relaxation and grain-growth effects.

contradictions.description: The boundary limits the hypothesis to processing conditions that achieve refinement without excessive coarsening or phase transformation, whereas the falsification rule treats failure to achieve a nanocrystalline structure as falsification rather than as failure to satisfy the stated applicability conditions.
